data.title: Build
data.tagline: A build converts source code, dependencies, and configuration into a runnable or releasable artifact.
data.learningOutcome: You can distinguish an identifiable build artifact from whether it has been deployed, verified, or opened to users.
data.description: Front-end source can build into a `dist` folder and service code into a versioned container image. A successful build means that commit produced the requested artifact. Making it available in testing or production is a later deployment and release step.

learning.assumes: You know source code must pass through a command or pipeline before others can run it.
learning.outcome: You can distinguish an identifiable build artifact from whether it has been deployed, verified, or opened to users.

distinctions.label: Deployment
distinctions.explanation: Build turns source into a runnable or releasable artifact. Deployment places a selected artifact into a target environment for intended users or systems.

explanation.title: An artifact fixes one source version
explanation.text: A build combines the commit, dependencies, and configuration into browser-loadable files or an image. A commit or version identifier tells the team what testing and deployment are using.

explanation.title: A successful build is not usable product evidence
explanation.text: It only proves an artifact was generated; it may not be deployed or may fail after deployment. Check the environment URL, test results, and release state separately.

data.boundary: Build is not deployment or release. Build makes an artifact; deployment places it in an environment; release makes it available to target users. One pipeline can perform all three, but each needs different evidence. The most common build failures beginners encounter are TypeScript type errors and missing imports. When the terminal shows 'Type error: Property X does not exist on type Y', it means the code tries to use a property or function that TypeScript doesn't know about. Sending the exact error message to AI is the fastest fix. Build errors block deployment - if build fails, nothing reaches the users.

lessonPractice.title: The pipeline says “Build succeeded,” but the test URL still shows the old page. Which judgment is correct?

options.label: Check this build's version and confirm whether the test environment actually deployed that same artifact
options.feedback: Correct. A build artifact and the version actually running in an environment are different things.

options.label: Run the build again, then refresh the test URL to see whether the old page gets replaced
options.feedback: Building again only produces another artifact. If deployment does not use it, the test environment can remain old.

options.label: Clear browser cache and treat seeing the new page as evidence that this build succeeded
options.feedback: Cache can affect what you see, but a page change does not prove which build it came from. Check the deployed artifact or version identifier.

data.agentPrompt: Generate a deployable build artifact for this commit and include its commit or version identifier in the result. Then tell me what the artifact is and whether it has reached the test environment; do not treat a successful build as release completion.
